# The Crossing: A Plan for Moving from Licenses to Subscriptions

## The Plan on Two Pages

*(The plan itself, suitable for adoption. Everything that follows is the reasoning and the machinery.)*

**Our posture.** The subscription must be a magnet, not a mandate. Customers who feel pushed will push back; customers who feel courted will come. We will never end-of-life what we sold as perpetual — a deed is a deed. The trough is not the risk; the *surprise* is. So we name the trough before it arrives, give it a shape we chose, and walk the board, our largest investors, our senior salespeople, and our top hundred accounts across the bridge before asking any of them to stand on it. Nothing in this plan is announced before it is consulted.

**The offer.** Three subscription tiers built around continuous delivery rather than version numbers. A **perpetual parachute**: after three consecutive subscribed years, a departing customer keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version, with twelve months of security maintenance — costed, scoped, and accounted for, not merely promised. A **heritage line**: perpetual remains available at a premium for regulated and government buyers, behind eligibility gates, a bookings cap, and an annual sunset review — an escape valve that makes the main path feel chosen. **Dual-run rights** for twelve months during cutover.

**The migration.** A published, declining credit schedule — generous in year one, thinner in year two, standard in year three. Gravity, not a wall; the market sets its own deadline. Credits, never discounts: the list price holds; the welcome expires. Upgrade amnesty for customers on old versions. Three-year price locks for early movers. Cohorts sequenced: new logos first, then upgrade-due customers, then maintenance customers, then the lapsed. A customer council consulted at the design stage, so the announcement ratifies what their input shaped.

**The pricing.** Subscription list priced at parity with each customer's annualized historical spend — license amortized, plus upgrades, plus maintenance — so budgets continue uninterrupted. The chosen shape: GAAP revenue down roughly 8% in year one, a trough of 20–25% across years two and three, inflection in year four, prior peak crossed in year five. Billings trough only half as deep, because annual prepay and multi-year locks pull cash forward. We considered a deeper, faster crossing and a shallower, slower one; we chose the middle deliberately, and we publish the choice.

**The compensation.** Reps are paid on the company we are building: commission on first-year contract value at signing, a renewal trail for years two and three, clawback on twelve-month churn, and a premium rate on multi-year prepaid deals — so the comp plan itself pulls cash into the trough. Migration conversions earn 1.3x quota credit in year one, declining with the credit schedule. Heritage deals earn half credit at a reduced rate, behind deal-desk approval — the loophole is legal but economically unattractive. A twenty-four-month income bridge guarantees floors so our best people are not asked to fund the transition personally.

**The investor plan.** We pre-announce the trough with its chosen shape and commit to it. Two quarters before launch, the scoreboard pivots to ARR, net revenue retention, billings, deferred revenue, and conversion coverage — before the old metrics deteriorate. We teach the accounting plainly: the trough is partly optical, because licenses recognized upfront become subscriptions recognized ratably, and cash will outrun GAAP revenue throughout. The board approves the transition with milestones and tripwires attached, and pre-agrees the responses to each tripwire — so a triggered response is execution, not improvisation.

**The entitlement charter.** Nothing you bought is taken; everything you bought is honored. Security patches for current and prior versions for five years, with published dates. Owed upgrades delivered, or converted to credit at 1.5x. Twelve months' notice before any end of support. The new thing is simply better.

**The governance.** A transition council — finance, sales, product, customer council delegate, investor relations — meets monthly, owns the credit schedule and heritage approvals, and answers tripwires. Leaders who drift toward the old model are approached first quietly, by respected peers. The plan itself is reviewed annually; anything that no longer earns its place is retired.

---

## Opening Framing

Our competitor did not lose a fifth of its installed base because it chose subscriptions. It lost them because it chose *surprise and coercion*: an announcement instead of a conversation, a deadline instead of a slope, a mandate where a magnet was needed. The lesson is not that transitions fail. It is that transitions imposed *at* stakeholders fail — and transitions built *with* them, patiently and in the right order, endure.

This plan therefore proceeds on a quiet premise: every constituency that could break the crossing — customers who feel entitled, salespeople who feel threatened, investors who feel alarmed — is consulted before it is asked, and given a dignified path before it is given a deadline. The sections below supply the machinery.

---

## 1. Strategic Posture: Three Failure Modes, One Path Between Them

- **The cliff.** Ending perpetual abruptly and forcing migration. This is the competitor's path: a 20% installed-base loss, concentrated — as such losses always are — among the customers with the most options.
- **The drift.** Offering both models indefinitely with no gravitational pull. The two-model company carries duplicate engineering, duplicate support, duplicate messaging — and never escapes. The deepest trough is the one that never ends.
- **The revolt.** Converting the pricing model without converting the people paid on the old one. A sales force compensated on large upfront deals will sabotage subscription selling quietly and completely, and top performers will leave at the exact moment the trough demands their best.

The path between them: **subscription-only for new customers from day one, gravity-based migration for the installed base, a comp plan rebuilt before the pricing plan ships, and a trough named before it arrives.**

---

## 2. The Offer: Tiers, a Parachute, and a Heritage Line

**Three tiers, one idea.** Standard, Professional, Enterprise — differentiated by capability, support depth, and deployment options, all built on continuous delivery. Version numbers retire. The product improves every month; the subscription is how you already have it.

**The perpetual parachute — priced, not just promised.** After three consecutive subscribed years, a customer who leaves keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version. Stress-tested before it ships:

- *Cost model.* Expected redemption is bounded: customers who have paid three years have already absorbed the switching cost, and most who leave would leave anyway — the parachute converts a bitter exit into a soft one and keeps the door open for return. We model redemption at 5–8% of the subscribed base; the liability is reviewed quarterly by the council.
- *Scope limits.* The parachute freezes at the then-current version, carries twelve months of security maintenance, and then support ends — a perpetual license without maintenance decays gracefully, and we say so plainly rather than letting the promise hollow out. Continued maintenance-only contracts are available at a premium.
- *Churn incentive at year three.* Answered structurally: renewal pricing improves with tenure, and the version a customer would parachute out on is always eighteen months behind the one subscribers are using.
- *Accounting.* The parachute is likely a material right under ASC 606 — a separate performance obligation requiring a slice of subscription revenue (modeled at 5–8%) to be deferred until vesting or expiry. We model this with our auditors *before* announcement, so the promise never becomes a restatement.
- *Anti-gaming.* The parachute vests once per account. Returning customers re-enter at standard pricing, not amnesty pricing.

**The heritage line — with guardrails.** Perpetual remains available, because some buyers (government, defense, regulated industries) have procurement regimes that genuinely require it — and because the visible existence of a chosen alternative makes the main path feel chosen. Guardrails: written eligibility criteria and deal-desk approval; pricing at 2.5–3x annual subscription upfront plus 22–25% annual maintenance, so five-year cost of ownership clearly favors subscription; a bookings cap (no more than 15% of quarterly bookings in year one, 10% in year two, 5% in year three, with excess requiring CFO sign-off); reduced commission, per Section 5; and an annual sunset review by the council. The heritage line is a valve, not a business.

**Dual-run rights.** Twelve months of parallel operation during cutover, standard. No migration should be a leap.

---

## 3. The Migration: Gravity, Not a Wall

**The declining credit schedule — published, not negotiated.** Year one: migration credits up to 60% of first-year subscription value, sized to the customer's remaining upgrade entitlement and paid-up maintenance. Year two: up to 40%. Year three: standard pricing. The schedule is public, so no customer is humiliated by a deadline they learned too late, and no rep can invent a better deal in a hallway.

**Credits, never discounts.** The list price is forever; the welcome is temporary. Discounting the subscription itself would set a low anchor that every renewal would re-fight. Crediting money already spent honors the past without mortgaging the future.

**Sequencing — the quiet order matters:**

- *Wave 0 (from launch):* New logos are subscription-only. No one's entitlement is touched; the model proves itself on uncontested ground.
- *Wave 1:* Customers due for a paid upgrade within twelve months — already budgeting, already expecting change.

# The Shape of Work: A Framework for a Global Company

## The Framework on Two Pages

*(The policy itself, suitable for adoption. Everything that follows is the reasoning and the machinery.)*

**Our posture.** Flexibility is the default; presence is a deliberate act, chosen for purpose. The office must earn the commute. We hold a small set of global anchors firmly, and we release the *how* to teams and regions — because the people closest to the work, consulted well, will shape it better than any central rule.

**The seven anchors — global, non-negotiable:**

1. **Outcomes over presence.** We evaluate results, not visibility.
2. **Equity of experience.** Location does not determine access to information, opportunity, or advancement.
3. **Documentation as default.** Decisions and rationale are written and discoverable.
4. **Time-zone respect.** Collaboration happens within cluster windows; the burden of inconvenient hours rotates.
5. **The right to disconnect.** Modeled by leadership; where it is law, obeyed.
6. **Security, compliance, and duty of care.** Labor law, working-time records, data residency, health-and-safety obligations at home and on site. No local workaround justifies a breach.
7. **Co-determination.** Works councils and employee representatives are consulted at the design stage, not the announcement stage.

**Local freedom.** Teams negotiate work charters — core hours, meeting norms, in-person cadence — within the anchors. Charters expire after twelve months unless renewed. Countries are grouped into six to eight clusters by time zone, labor-law regime, and working norms: one policy per cluster, not one per country, not one for the world.

**Pay.** Roles are benchmarked to local labor markets, and the band logic is published internally. Relocation changes pay only at defined thresholds, with notice and transition — never retroactively. Pay compression between clusters is reviewed annually.

**When we disagree.** Individuals whose needs conflict with a charter have a defined accommodation path. Interdependent teams whose charters collide resolve them within a cluster coordination window. Leaders who drift from the anchors are approached first quietly, by respected peers; a standing framework council adjudicates what quiet correction cannot resolve.

**What we measure.** System health in aggregate — belonging, attrition, promotion equity, network health, space use. Never individual surveillance: no keystrokes, no screenshots, no online-status tracking, no camera-on monitoring.

**What we fund.** Home-office setup and connectivity for remote staff; predictable scheduling and shift autonomy for site-based staff; a deliberate gathering budget; office redesign where utilization data supports it.

**How this changes.** Annually, by the framework council, after consultation in every cluster. Anything that no longer earns its place is retired.

---

## Opening Framing

Most future-of-work debates open with: *how many days should people be in the office?* A more useful starting question is: **what is presence *for* — and what is distance *for*?** Answer those honestly, together, and the days-per-week argument largely resolves itself.

The framework below rests on a quiet premise: employees are not resources to be located but people to be trusted — and the company, in each of its countries, is a guest. A guest in local cultures, local laws, local lives. Work designed *at* people tends to fail slowly and then suddenly, usually visible first in the resignation letters of those with the most options. Work designed *with* people endures.

The design principle: **anchor the why, release the how.** And a second principle, just as important: **consult before you announce.** A framework of this kind cannot survive its own unveiling unless the ground has been prepared — with employee representatives, works councils, country leadership, and respected senior figures whose quiet endorsement carries more weight than any launch email. The sections that follow are written to be built by consensus, because a framework built by consultation will be defended by the people who built it.

---

## 1. Strategic Posture: Presence as a Deliberate Act

The workable position is **structured flexibility**: flexibility is the default; presence is chosen for purpose. Two failure modes sit on either side, and both are worth naming with care:

- **The mandate trap.** Blanket return-to-office rules buy visible compliance at the price of quiet attrition — and quiet resentment, which is harder to repair. The evidence is accumulating: the Trip.com randomized trial (Bloom et al., *Nature*, 2024; 1,612 employees) found hybrid arrangements cut attrition by roughly a third with no measurable cost to performance or promotion. Mandates also send a signal that is difficult to unsend: *we manage what we can see.*
- **The drift trap.** Fully distributed by default, with no deliberate gathering, erodes the weak ties that carry culture, mentoring, and unexpected ideas. Isolation arrives quietly and is usually noticed late.

The posture between them: **the office must earn the commute.** Magnet, not mandate. An office people choose to enter is telling you something; an office people are required to enter is telling you something else.

---

## 2. The Anchors: Global Non-Negotiables

Keep this list short — seven items, no more. Everything beyond it is local.

1. **Outcomes over presence.** Hours online are a proxy for those who cannot articulate what they actually want produced.
2. **Equity of experience.** Location must not determine access to information, opportunity, or advancement. This is the anchor most often stated and least often enforced — Section 3 exists because of that.
3. **Documentation as default.** In a company spanning time zones, if it isn't written down, it happened to only some of us.
4. **Time-zone respect.** Defined collaboration windows per cluster; the burden of the 7am and the 10pm rotates. Inconvenience that always falls on the same country is a policy, whether or not it is written anywhere.
5. **The right to disconnect.** Modeled by leadership, not merely published. In a growing list of jurisdictions — France since 2017, Portugal since 2021, and others moving — this is law, not philosophy.
6. **Security, compliance, and duty of care.** Data residency, local labor law, works-council obligations — and two items frameworks too often miss: **mandatory working-time recording** (the CJEU's 2019 *CCOO v. Deutsche Bank* ruling, Spain's daily time-registry requirement, and Germany's working-time documentation obligations constrain flexible-hours design more than any right-to-disconnect law) and **health-and-safety duty of care extending to the home office** (a legal obligation in several jurisdictions; Germany's statutory accident insurance has covered home working since 2021). Freedom ends where the law begins.
7. **Co-determination, consulted early.** In Germany, France, the Netherlands, and elsewhere, works councils hold real legal rights over working-time and monitoring arrangements. Bring them in at the design stage, and their judgment shapes the framework; bring them in at the announcement stage, and their judgment shapes the obstruction.

---

## 3. Governing the Framework: Guardianship, Quiet Correction, and Accommodation

An anchor without machinery is a wish. This section supplies the machinery — designed, deliberately, to preserve relationships while it enforces principles.

- **A small framework council.** Representatives from every cluster, employee and works-council delegates, HR, facilities, and IT. Its authority rests on legitimacy and consultative process, not on size. It meets quarterly, owns the anchors, adjudicates disputes, and leads the annual renewal.
- **Quiet correction first.** When a senior leader drifts from the posture — a country head mandating five days in office, for instance — the first response is a private conversation with a respected peer or the council chair. Alignment is sought before anything is escalated; face is preserved; most drift resolves at this stage, and the relationship survives the correction.
- **A defined path when quiet correction fails.** Council review, then the executive sponsor, with a decision inside thirty days. Genuine exceptions are possible — but they must be time-bound, justified in writing, and logged. Exceptions that are visible stay rare; exceptions that are hidden become precedent.
- **An accommodation path for individuals.** Team charters are collective agreements, but lives are individual. When a person's needs conflict with the charter — caregiving, health, disability, religious observance — the path is: a conversation with the manager; a charter review if the need is shared by others; a formal accommodation through HR with a written outcome; and, finally, appeal to the council. No one should have to choose between their life and their team's default settings.
- **The framework sunsets too.** It expires annually unless renewed by the council after cluster consultation. A living document, not a monument.

---

## 4. Release the How: Charters, Clusters, and the Spaces Between Teams

- **Team work charters.** Each team negotiates its own rhythms — core hours, meeting norms, in-person cadence, response expectations — within the anchors. Charters carry **sunset clauses**: they expire after twelve months unless renewed. Norms that never expire quietly become the new bureaucracy.
- **Country clusters, not 190 policies.** Group locations by time zone, labor-law regime, and working-culture norms — likely six to eight clusters. One policy per country is unmanageable; one policy for the world is dishonest.
- **The advice process, with its failure modes addressed.** Decisions are made by those closest to the problem, after seeking advice from those affected and those with relevant expertise. Senior review, prepared well, is wisdom rather than delay — the discipline is to bring experienced leaders in early, so their judgment shapes the design rather than merely stamping it. Two known failure modes deserve explicit guardrails: **decision paralysis** is answered with time-boxed advice windows (advice is sought for ten working days; then the decider decides), and **unclear tie-breaking** is answered by naming the decider in advance, in the charter itself. The advice process requires consultation, not unanimity.
- **Charter collisions between interdependent teams.** Charters assume teams are autonomous; reality disagrees. Three mechanisms: each cluster sets a **coordination window** — three to four overlapping hours that no charter may override; cross-team dependencies are **mapped at charter signing**, so collisions surface before they hurt; and a quarterly **charter fair** lets interdependent teams renegotiate together, with the council's coordination panel resolving what the room cannot.

---

## 5. Cultural Attunement: The Quiet Core

This is the section on which everything else silently depends — and a caution before it begins: **what follows describes tendencies, not destinies.** Variation within any country — generational, regional, individual — routinely exceeds the variation between national averages. Use cultural frameworks as questions, never as answers; the colleague in front of you is not an average.

- **Meaning travels differently.** In some cultures meaning sits in the words; in others it sits around them. A "yes" can mean *I agree*, *I hear you*, or *I will not be the one to say no in this meeting.* Silence can signal respect, dissent, or processing. Training for this is not a soft extra; it is operational infrastructure.
- **Hierarchy expectations vary.** Some teams expect the manager to decide; others expect consensus built quietly before the meeting ever convenes — the Japanese practice of *nemawashi*, where the formal meeting ratifies an agreement already built, is one elegant example. Neither mode is wrong. Designing for one and imposing it on all is.
- **Feedback styles differ sharply.** Directness that one culture reads as refreshing candor, another may receive as wounding; politeness that one reads as respect, another may read as opacity. Global feedback frameworks should be calibrated locally, or they will calibrate people instead.
- **Calendars are not universal.** Weekends do not fall on Saturday–Sunday everywhere; Ramadan, Lunar New Year, Golden Week, and dozens of national rhythms shape the working year. Scheduling systems should know this without being told twice.
- **Listen for what is not said.** In high-context cultures, the important signal rarely arrives through a 1–5 engagement-survey scale. Supplement surveys with trusted local facilitators, informal settings, and cultural advisors in each cluster — people whose role is partly to translate the silence.

---

## 6. The Office, Reimagined: From Obligation to Destination

- **Treat the office as a product.** It has users, a value proposition, and competitors — the kitchen table among them. Design it for what distance does poorly: spontaneous collision, mentoring osmosis, celebration, difficult conversations, creative sprints.
- **Shift the space mix.** Fewer assigned desks; more collaboration zones, quiet rooms, and a genuine social heart. Bookable and adaptable rather than fixed.
- **Local meaning varies.** In some cities the office is prestige,

Genuine exceptions are possible — but they must be time-bound, justified in writing, and logged. Exceptions that are visible stay rare; exceptions that are hidden become precedent.
- **An accommodation path for individuals.** Team charters are collective agreements, but lives are individual. When a person's needs conflict with the charter — caregiving, health, disability, religious observance — the path is: a conversation with the manager; a charter review if the need is shared by others; a formal accommodation through HR with a written outcome; and, finally, appeal to the council. No one should have to choose between their life and their team's default settings.
- **The framework sunsets too.** It expires annually unless renewed by the council after cluster consultation. A living document, not a monument.

---

## 4. Release the How: Charters, Clusters, and the Spaces Between Teams

- **Team work charters.** Each team negotiates its own rhythms — core hours, meeting norms, in-person cadence, response expectations — within the anchors. Charters carry **sunset clauses**: they expire after twelve months unless renewed. Norms that never expire quietly become the new bureaucracy.
- **Country clusters, not 190 policies.** Group locations by time zone, labor-law regime, and working-culture norms — likely six to eight clusters. One policy per country is unmanageable; one policy for the world is dishonest.
- **The advice process, with its failure modes addressed.** Decisions are made by those closest to the problem, after seeking advice from those affected and those with relevant expertise. Senior review, prepared well, is wisdom rather than delay — the discipline is to bring experienced leaders in early, so their judgment shapes the design rather than merely stamping it. Two known failure modes deserve explicit guardrails: **decision paralysis** is answered with time-boxed advice windows (advice is sought for ten working days; then the decider decides), and **unclear tie-breaking** is answered by naming the decider in advance, in the charter itself. The advice process requires consultation, not unanimity.
- **Charter collisions between interdependent teams.** Charters assume teams are autonomous; reality disagrees. Three mechanisms: each cluster sets a **coordination window** — three to four overlapping hours that no charter may override; cross-team dependencies are **mapped at charter signing**, so collisions surface before they hurt; and a quarterly **charter fair** lets interdependent teams renegotiate together, with the council's coordination panel resolving what the room cannot.

---

## 5. Cultural Attunement: The Quiet Core

This is the section on which everything else silently depends — and a caution before it begins: **what follows describes tendencies, not destinies.** Variation within any country — generational, regional, individual — routinely exceeds the variation between national averages. Use cultural frameworks as questions, never as answers; the colleague in front of you is not an average.

- **Meaning travels differently.** In some cultures meaning sits in the words; in others it sits around them. A "yes" can mean *I agree*, *I hear you*, or *I will not be the one to say no in this meeting.* Silence can signal respect, dissent, or processing. Training for this is not a soft extra; it is operational infrastructure.
- **Hierarchy expectations vary.** Some teams expect the manager to decide; others expect consensus built quietly before the meeting ever convenes — the Japanese practice of *nemawashi*, where the formal meeting ratifies an agreement already built, is one elegant example. Neither mode is wrong. Designing for one and imposing it on all is.
- **Feedback styles differ sharply.** Directness that one culture reads as refreshing candor, another may receive as wounding; politeness that one reads as respect, another may read as opacity. Global feedback frameworks should be calibrated locally, or they will calibrate people instead.
- **Calendars are not universal.** Weekends do not fall on Saturday–Sunday everywhere; Ramadan, Lunar New Year, Golden Week, and dozens of national rhythms shape the working year. Scheduling systems should know this without being told twice.
- **Listen for what is not said.** In high-context cultures, the important signal rarely arrives through a 1–5 engagement-survey scale. Supplement surveys with trusted local facilitators, informal settings, and cultural advisors in each cluster — people whose role is partly to translate the silence.

---

## 6. The Office, Reimagined: From Obligation to Destination

- **Treat the office as a product.** It has users, a value proposition, and competitors — the kitchen table among them. Design it for what distance does poorly: spontaneous collision, mentoring osmosis, celebration, difficult conversations, creative sprints.
- **Shift the space mix.** Fewer assigned desks; more collaboration zones, quiet rooms, and a genuine social heart. Bookable and adaptable rather than fixed.
- **Local meaning varies.** In some cities the office is prestige,

# Critique: "The Crossing" — License-to-Subscription Transition Plan

## The Blocking Problem

The output is **truncated mid-sentence** ("A customer council consulted at the design—"). As submitted, it covers the offer structure and part of the migration design — roughly one and a half of the four deliverables explicitly requested. Pricing, sales compensation, and the investor communication plan are absent. This alone prevents a pass.

## What Works (Credit Where Due)

- **"Magnet, not mandate"** draws the correct lesson from the competitor's 20% installed-base loss.
- **The perpetual parachute** (own the current version after three subscribed years) is a genuinely innovative adoption de-risker.
- **The heritage line** is a clever escape valve — it preserves the psychology of choice while segmenting regulated/government buyers.
- **The declining credit schedule** ("gravity, not a wall") lets the market self-sequence migration without a coercive cliff.
- **"A deed is a deed"** correctly defuses the entitlement grievance at the principle level.

**1. Sales compensation redesign is missing entirely.** The prompt flags this as a structural blocker: reps paid on large upfront deals will actively sabotage subscription selling. Required and absent: ARR-based or trailing multi-year payout, accelerators for migration deals, renewal-linked components, treatment of heritage-line sales, and an 18–24 month comp bridge so top performers don't defect mid-trough.

**2. No pricing analysis of the trough tradeoff.** The prompt explicitly asks for pricing that balances trough depth against adoption. There are no numbers, no scenarios, no anchoring (e.g., subscription priced against customers' historical annualized license-plus-upgrade spend), no annual-prepay mechanics to pull cash forward, and no stated choice between deep-discount-fast-adoption versus shallow-discount-slower-transition. This is the analytical heart of the request and it isn't here.

**3. No financial communication plan.** The fourth deliverable is wholly absent. Needed: pre-announcing the trough with a chosen shape (depth, duration, inflection year); pivoting the investor scoreboard to ARR, NRR, billings, and deferred revenue *before* the old metrics deteriorate; the ASC 606 explanation that the trough is partly optical — upfront license recognition vs. ratable subscription means cash and billings will outrun GAAP revenue; and pre-committed board milestones with agreed tripwires.

**4. The parachute is unpriced.** Granting a perpetual license after three years creates a contingent liability and a built-in churn incentive at year three. It needs cost modeling, version-scope limits, and an explicit support window — a perpetual license without maintenance decays, and if that's the intent, say so or the promise is hollow.

**5. The heritage line has no guardrails.** Keeping perpetual available gives the sales force a loophole to keep selling what they're currently paid on, and gives investors reason to doubt commitment. Define eligibility criteria, premium magnitude, and a sunset review date.

**6. No sequencing or segmentation.** Which cohorts migrate first — new logos, renewal-due upgraders, lapsed customers? What installed-base coverage is targeted by year, and what attrition ceiling triggers intervention? The competitor's 20% loss demands a defined early-warning metric.

**7. Entitlement handled only at principle level.** How long are old versions patched? Security-only support windows? What do customers mid-contract on paid upgrades receive? "A deed is a deed" doesn't answer the operational questions that determine whether the installed base feels honored or abandoned.

## Required Revisions

1. Complete the document — restore everything after the truncation point.
2. Add a quantified pricing section with 2–3 trough-depth/adoption scenarios and a defended choice.
3. Add the full compensation redesign, including the transition bridge.
4. Add the investor/board plan: metric pivot, accounting framing, pre-committed milestones and tripwires.
5. Stress-test the parachute and heritage line for cost and loopholes before locking them in.

The strategic instincts in the visible portion are strong — this is a good opening third of a plan, not a plan.

Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS

# The Crossing: A Plan for Moving from Licenses to Subscriptions

## The Plan on Two Pages

*(The plan itself, suitable for adoption. Everything that follows is the reasoning and the machinery.)*

**Our posture.** The subscription must be a magnet, not a mandate. Customers who feel pushed will push back; customers who feel courted will come. We will never end-of-life what we sold as perpetual — a deed is a deed. The trough is not the risk; the *surprise* is. So we name the trough before it arrives, give it a shape we chose, and walk the board, our largest investors, our senior salespeople, and our top hundred accounts across the bridge before asking any of them to stand on it. Nothing in this plan is announced before it is consulted.

**The offer.** Three subscription tiers built around continuous delivery rather than version numbers. A **perpetual parachute**: after three consecutive subscribed years, a departing customer keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version, with twelve months of security maintenance — costed, scoped, and accounted for, not merely promised. A **heritage line**: perpetual remains available at a premium for regulated and government buyers, behind eligibility gates, a bookings cap, and an annual sunset review — an escape valve that makes the main path feel chosen. **Dual-run rights** for twelve months during cutover.

**The migration.** A published, declining credit schedule — generous in year one, thinner in year two, standard in year three. Gravity, not a wall; the market sets its own deadline. Credits, never discounts: the list price holds; the welcome expires. Upgrade amnesty for customers on old versions. Three-year price locks for early movers. Cohorts sequenced: new logos first, then upgrade-due customers, then maintenance customers, then the lapsed. A customer council consulted at the design stage, so the announcement ratifies what their input shaped.

**The pricing.** Subscription list priced at parity with each customer's annualized historical spend — license amortized, plus upgrades, plus maintenance — so budgets continue uninterrupted. The chosen shape: GAAP revenue down roughly 8% in year one, a trough of 20–25% across years two and three, inflection in year four, prior peak crossed in year five. Billings trough only half as deep, because annual prepay and multi-year locks pull cash forward. We considered a deeper, faster crossing and a shallower, slower one; we chose the middle deliberately, and we publish the choice.

**The compensation.** Reps are paid on the company we are building: commission on first-year contract value at signing, a renewal trail for years two and three, clawback on twelve-month churn, and a premium rate on multi-year prepaid deals — so the comp plan itself pulls cash into the trough. Migration conversions earn 1.3x quota credit in year one, declining with the credit schedule. Heritage deals earn half credit at a reduced rate, behind deal-desk approval — the loophole is legal but economically unattractive. A twenty-four-month income bridge guarantees floors so our best people are not asked to fund the transition personally.

**The investor plan.** We pre-announce the trough with its chosen shape and commit to it. Two quarters before launch, the scoreboard pivots to ARR, net revenue retention, billings, deferred revenue, and conversion coverage — before the old metrics deteriorate. We teach the accounting plainly: the trough is partly optical, because licenses recognized upfront become subscriptions recognized ratably, and cash will outrun GAAP revenue throughout. The board approves the transition with milestones and tripwires attached, and pre-agrees the responses to each tripwire — so a triggered response is execution, not improvisation.

**The entitlement charter.** Nothing you bought is taken; everything you bought is honored. Security patches for current and prior versions for five years, with published dates. Owed upgrades delivered, or converted to credit at 1.5x. Twelve months' notice before any end of support. The new thing is simply better.

**The governance.** A transition council — finance, sales, product, customer council delegate, investor relations — meets monthly, owns the credit schedule and heritage approvals, and answers tripwires. Leaders who drift toward the old model are approached first quietly, by respected peers. The plan itself is reviewed annually; anything that no longer earns its place is retired.

---

## Opening Framing

Our competitor did not lose a fifth of its installed base because it chose subscriptions. It lost them because it chose *surprise and coercion*: an announcement instead of a conversation, a deadline instead of a slope, a mandate where a magnet was needed. The lesson is not that transitions fail. It is that transitions imposed *at* stakeholders fail — and transitions built *with* them, patiently and in the right order, endure.

This plan therefore proceeds on a quiet premise: every constituency that could break the crossing — customers who feel entitled, salespeople who feel threatened, investors who feel alarmed — is consulted before it is asked, and given a dignified path before it is given a deadline. The sections below supply the machinery.

---

## 1. Strategic Posture: Three Failure Modes, One Path Between Them

- **The cliff.** Ending perpetual abruptly and forcing migration. This is the competitor's path: a 20% installed-base loss, concentrated — as such losses always are — among the customers with the most options.
- **The drift.** Offering both models indefinitely with no gravitational pull. The two-model company carries duplicate engineering, duplicate support, duplicate messaging — and never escapes. The deepest trough is the one that never ends.
- **The revolt.** Converting the pricing model without converting the people paid on the old one. A sales force compensated on large upfront deals will sabotage subscription selling quietly and completely, and top performers will leave at the exact moment the trough demands their best.

The path between them: **subscription-only for new customers from day one, gravity-based migration for the installed base, a comp plan rebuilt before the pricing plan ships, and a trough named before it arrives.**

---

## 2. The Offer: Tiers, a Parachute, and a Heritage Line

**Three tiers, one idea.** Standard, Professional, Enterprise — differentiated by capability, support depth, and deployment options, all built on continuous delivery. Version numbers retire. The product improves every month; the subscription is how you already have it.

**The perpetual parachute — priced, not just promised.** After three consecutive subscribed years, a customer who leaves keeps a perpetual license to the then-current version. Stress-tested before it ships:

- *Cost model.* Expected redemption is bounded: customers who have paid three years have already absorbed the switching cost, and most who leave would leave anyway — the parachute converts a bitter exit into a soft one and keeps the door open for return. We model redemption at 5–8% of the subscribed base; the liability is reviewed quarterly by the council.
- *Scope limits.* The parachute freezes at the then-current version, carries twelve months of security maintenance, and then support ends — a perpetual license without maintenance decays gracefully, and we say so plainly rather than letting the promise hollow out. Continued maintenance-only contracts are available at a premium.
- *Churn incentive at year three.* Answered structurally: renewal pricing improves with tenure, and the version a customer would parachute out on is always eighteen months behind the one subscribers are using.
- *Accounting.* The parachute is likely a material right under ASC 606 — a separate performance obligation requiring a slice of subscription revenue (modeled at 5–8%) to be deferred until vesting or expiry. We model this with our auditors *before* announcement, so the promise never becomes a restatement.
- *Anti-gaming.* The parachute vests once per account. Returning customers re-enter at standard pricing, not amnesty pricing.

**The heritage line — with guardrails.** Perpetual remains available, because some buyers (government, defense, regulated industries) have procurement regimes that genuinely require it — and because the visible existence of a chosen alternative makes the main path feel chosen. Guardrails: written eligibility criteria and deal-desk approval; pricing at 2.5–3x annual subscription upfront plus 22–25% annual maintenance, so five-year cost of ownership clearly favors subscription; a bookings cap (no more than 15% of quarterly bookings in year one, 10% in year two, 5% in year three, with excess requiring CFO sign-off); reduced commission, per Section 5; and an annual sunset review by the council. The heritage line is a valve, not a business.

**Dual-run rights.** Twelve months of parallel operation during cutover, standard. No migration should be a leap.

---

## 3. The Migration: Gravity, Not a Wall

**The declining credit schedule — published, not negotiated.** Year one: migration credits up to 60% of first-year subscription value, sized to the customer's remaining upgrade entitlement and paid-up maintenance. Year two: up to 40%. Year three: standard pricing. The schedule is public, so no customer is humiliated by a deadline they learned too late, and no rep can invent a better deal in a hallway.

**Credits, never discounts.** The list price is forever; the welcome is temporary. Discounting the subscription itself would set a low anchor that every renewal would re-fight. Crediting money already spent honors the past without mortgaging the future.

**Sequencing — the quiet order matters:**

- *Wave 0 (from launch):* New logos are subscription-only. No one's entitlement is touched; the model proves itself on uncontested ground.
- *Wave 1:* Customers due for a paid upgrade within twelve months — already budgeting, already expecting change.
